newsitem.title: USA: Dlr starts US below peaks after surging overseas.
newsitem.headline: Dlr starts US below peaks after surging overseas.

text.p: The dollar began U.S. trade robust, but below fresh overseas peaks, after being swept higher against the mark, Swiss franc and yen by a wave of bullish momentum which showed no signs of dissipating.

The greenback surged through key resistance at 1.8430 marks, touching a high of 1.8473 marks in early Europe -- its top level against the mark since November 1989 -- and popped above 117 yen to a two-and-a-half month peak of 117.42 yen.
Dealers said profit-taking could stall the dollar rally in early New York trade, but saw little reason to bet against a continuation of the greenback's spectacular run.

"If anything, you might see a little bit of a pullback this morning on profit-taking, but then I expect the trend to continue," said Ricardo Gomes, foreign exchange manager at Republic National Bank of New York.
"I think the only thing that stops the dollar now is an EMU delay and obviously European politicians are doing everything they can to avoid that," he added.
The dollar debuted at 1.8422/32 marks, up from 1.8368/78 at the close of trading on Friday. It was changing hands at 117.00/10 yen at the outset of trading against 116.82/92 on Friday.
After surging to a four-year peak of 1.5250 Swiss francs, the dollar shrank back to open only slightly higher at 1.5063/68 against 1.5155/65.

In the wake of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's upbeat Humphrey-Hawkins testimony last week, dealers said a sharp dollar/mark rally had spread into broad dollar rally, based as much on strong U.S. fundamentals as sluggish European growth.
Strategists are now targetting 2.00 marks per dollar and fears the Bundesbank could surprise the market with inter- meeting action on the repo rate appeared to be dwindling.

"Germany really doesn't have much to worry about with this move up in dollar/mark," said David Gilmore, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics, noting that Bundesbank members had expressed little concern about the prospects for imported inflation as a result of the weak mark.
"Export demand is really their only ticket for bringing the Maastricht criteria within reach."
Traders characterized dollar prospects against the yen as positive but limited given the contentious nature of trade relations between the U.S. and Japan.

They downplayed the importance of several key U.S. economic reports due later this week, noting that Greenspan's resounding endorsement of U.S. growth and inflation prospects was enough to support the greenback in the near-term, regardless of the data.
On Tuesday, the Labor Department will release its Employment Cost Index for the second quarter, an important gauge of inflation pressures.
Other key indicators include an advanced reading of second quarter GDP Thursday and employment and National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) reports for July on Friday.
"It's going to take quite a lot to move Greenspan and so unless these numbers are really way out of whack I don't think it slows down dollar momentum," said Republic's Gomes.
In other trade on Monday, sterling slumped sharply against the mark in morning trade, triggering stop-loss sell orders and spilling over into a weaker cable rate.
Sterling/dollar opened at $1.6510/20, down sharply from Friday's closing rate of $1.6645/55, but stumbled as low as $1.64 -- its lowest level since mid-June -- as the morning unfolded.
Elsewhere, the dollar opened slightly stronger at Canadian $1.3850/55 against $1.3843/48 on Friday. The Australian dollar shrank to $0.7352/57 from $0.7377/82.
(( -- Noah Barkin, N.A. Forex Unit, 212-859-1673 ))
